blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the complexity of understanding consistency models across distributed systems, databases, and computer architecture, noting how terminology differs between communities and how easy it is to forget nuances over time. The paper by Aguilera and Terry introduces a framework for thinking about consistency through two lenses: state consistency (invariants on system state) and operation consistency (constraints on observable operation results). The key insight is that operation consistency is an end-to-end property that can hide underlying state inconsistencies, as demonstrated by an example where reads from a majority of replicas still provide strong consistency despite temporary state inconsistencies. The paper also attempts to unify terminology across disciplines, clarifying how different communities interpret consistency, isolation, and atomicity.
paper_venue: IEEE Transactions on Data Engineering Bulletin
paper_abstract: The notion of consistency is used across diﬀerent computer science disciplines from distributed systems to database systems to computer architecture. It turns out that consistency can mean quite diﬀerent things across these disciplines, depending on who uses it and in what context it appears. We identify two broad types of consistency, state consistency and operation consistency, which diﬀer fundamentally in meaning and scope. We explain how these types map to the many examples of consistency in each discipline.
